quizzes.title: Key terms and ideas
quizzes.intro: Ten quick checks on what the course covers, how it is graded and the basic words a weaving engineer uses.

questions.q: What is the course code of Weaving Calculations in this outline?
questions.explain: The outline is headed Course Outline – Weaving Calculations (TX-416). TC is the abbreviation used for Textile Costing, a different course.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT listed among the course outcomes?
options: Planning a weaving factory to meet customer orders
questions.explain: The three stated outcomes are productivity of weaving machines, planning a weaving factory for customer orders, and fabric weight and cover. Dyeing recipes belong to wet processing, not this course.

questions.q: Which assessment carries the largest share of the final grade?
questions.explain: The final examination carries 30 marks; quizzes and the mid term carry 25 each, and participation and assignments 10 each.

questions.q: Participation and assignments together are worth the same as the mid term.
questions.explain: Participation (10) plus assignments (10) make 20 marks, while the mid term alone is worth 25 marks.

questions.q: What does a yarn count express?
options: The number of fibres in a yarn
questions.explain: A count is a number that expresses how fine or coarse a yarn is, either as length per weight (Ne, Nm) or weight per length (tex, denier). Twist and strength are measured separately.

questions.q: In the plan, which operation comes between warping and the loom when a warp is being prepared?
questions.explain: Weaving preparation runs cones → warping → sizing → drawing-in → loom; sizing coats the warp so it survives weaving. Carding is a spinning process and singeing and mercerising are wet-processing steps.

questions.q: The term GSM in the lecture on fabric weight stands for what?
questions.explain: GSM is grams per square metre, the usual metric fabric weight; the same lecture also covers oz/yd² and weight per linear metre.

questions.q: The outline says the course deals mainly with the chemistry of sizing and dyeing.
questions.explain: The description is about the calculations a weaving engineer performs: counts, fabric weight and cover, preparation, loom production, planning and feasibility. Sizing appears only as a cost-analysis topic.

questions.q: Which lecture would you open to learn how many metres a loom weaves in a day?
questions.explain: Fabric Production (week 7) covers loom output from picks per minute, picks per inch and efficiency. Cone size, reed and counting systems deal with yarn packages, reed dents and yarn numbering.

questions.q: What is the attendance threshold below which a student receives an F grade?
questions.explain: The rule states that attendance below 80 % means an F grade, because the calculations build on each other week by week.

quizzes.title: Formulas and relationships
quizzes.intro: How the grading weights, the weekly plan and the basic yarn and fabric measures relate to one another.

questions.q: The five grading components (10, 10, 25, 25, 30) add up to how many marks?
questions.explain: 10 + 10 + 25 + 25 + 30 = 100, so each component is directly a percentage of the final grade.

questions.q: In an indirect count system such as Ne, a finer yarn has a:
questions.explain: Indirect systems measure length per unit weight; a finer yarn gives more length for the same weight, so the number rises. In direct systems (tex, denier) the number falls.

questions.q: If the loom speed in picks per minute rises and everything else stays the same, the metres woven per day will:
questions.explain: Production per day is proportional to picks per minute × efficiency ÷ picks per inch; more picks per minute insert more weft and so more length per day.

questions.q: With two lectures per week over 15 weeks the plan contains 30 lecture slots.
questions.explain: 15 weeks × 2 lectures = 30 slots; two of them are taken by the mid term and the overview.

questions.q: Which pair of lectures deals with the same topic at two levels of difficulty?
options: Cover Factor I and Cover Factor II
Blended Fabrics and Sizing Cost Analysis
questions.explain: Cover Factor I (week 6) and Cover Factor II — weavability on airjet (week 7) build on each other; the other pairs are different topics that happen to be adjacent.

questions.q: Fabric weight in GSM rises when which of these increases, other things equal?
questions.explain: More threads per inch of a given count means more yarn, and so more grams, in each square metre. Loom speed, efficiency and loom numbers affect output, not weight per square metre.

questions.q: In the outline, what happens to the mid-term and final weights if quizzes are removed from the scheme?
options: They together make 55 of the remaining 75 marks
They together make 55 of the remaining 100 marks
They together make 50 of the remaining 75 marks
They together make 30 of the remaining 75 marks
questions.explain: Mid term 25 + final 30 = 55; removing the 25 quiz marks leaves 100 − 25 = 75, so the two exams would be 55 of 75.

questions.q: In the direct tex system a coarser yarn has a lower number.
questions.explain: Tex is grams per 1,000 m; a coarser yarn weighs more per 1,000 m, so its tex is higher. The number falls for finer yarn.

questions.q: Attendance is counted on lectures held. Missing n lectures out of 30 keeps a student above the 80 % line only while n is at most:
questions.explain: 80 % of 30 is 24 lectures, so a student may miss 30 − 24 = 6 lectures. Missing 7 gives 23/30 = 76.7 %, below the line.

questions.q: Cover factor, introduced in weeks 6 and 7, describes:
options: How much of the fabric area is covered by yarn
The weight of size on the warp
The number of looms in a set
The price of one hank of yarn
questions.explain: Cover factor combines thread spacing and yarn diameter to say how closely the threads fill the fabric area; it governs weavability on airjet looms.

quizzes.title: Worked calculations
quizzes.intro: Small calculations on grades, attendance and the units (pounds, yards, maunds) that the course will use from week one.

questions.q: A student scores 8/10 participation, 7/10 assignments, 20/25 quizzes, 18/25 mid term and 24/30 final. What is the total out of 100?
questions.explain: Each component is already weighted, so simply add: 8 + 7 + 20 + 18 + 24 = 77 marks.

questions.q: A student averages 80 % across all the quizzes. How many of the 25 quiz marks does she earn?
questions.explain: 80 % of 25 = 0.8 × 25 = 20 marks towards the final grade.

questions.q: The course has 30 lectures. What is the minimum number a student must attend to reach exactly 80 % attendance?
questions.explain: 80 % of 30 = 0.8 × 30 = 24 lectures; attending 23 gives 76.7 % and an F grade.

questions.q: A student attends 23 of 30 lectures. What is his attendance percentage, to one decimal place?
questions.explain: 23 ÷ 30 × 100 = 76.7 %, which is below the 80 % threshold.

questions.q: The mid term is in week 8. How many lecture slots of teaching are there before it?
questions.explain: Weeks 1 to 7 are complete teaching weeks with 2 lectures each: 7 × 2 = 14 lectures before the mid term.

questions.q: Yarn is bought in pounds. Convert 5 lb to grams, taking 1 lb = 453.6 g.
Cotton is traded in maunds of 40 kg. How many kilograms are in 25 maunds?
questions.explain: 25 maunds × 40 kg = 1,000 kg, i.e. one tonne.

questions.q: A hank of cotton yarn is 840 yd. How many metres is that, taking 1 yd = 0.9144 m? Answer to one decimal place.
questions.explain: 840 × 0.9144 = 768.1 m; this figure is the basis of the constant 590.67 in Lecture 01.

questions.q: A student has 9 + 9 + 22 + 20 before the final. What final score (out of 30) gives exactly 80 in total?
questions.explain: 9 + 9 + 22 + 20 = 60, so 80 − 60 = 20 marks are needed in the final.

questions.q: Fabric is sold by the yard. A 100-yd piece is how many metres?
questions.explain: 100 × 0.9144 = 91.44 m. Dividing by 0.9144 instead gives 109.4, which would be yards in 100 m.

quizzes.title: Applied in practice
quizzes.intro: Which part of the course answers which day-to-day question in a weaving mill, plus some sensible study decisions.

questions.q: A buyer asks for the oz/yd² of a fabric you quote in GSM. Which lecture gives the conversion?
questions.explain: Weight of Fabric (week 3) covers GSM, oz/yd² and linear weight. Reed, cone and set-size lectures do not deal with fabric weight.

questions.q: The warp keeps breaking on the loom and the sizing manager blames the yarn. Which lecture helps you quantify the problem?
questions.explain: Breakages – Sized Count (week 4) deals with warp breaks and the count after sizing. Warping speed and crimp are different calculations; feasibility is about the plant.

questions.q: An order of 50,000 m must be delivered in six weeks and you need to know how many looms to allot. Which group of lectures applies?
questions.explain: The Planning lectures (weeks 10–12) deal with orders, loom changeovers, yarn for the looms and production over months. Counts and cover factor describe the yarn and fabric, not the schedule.

questions.q: Management wants to know whether a new 100-loom plant would pay. Which lecture would you prepare from?
questions.explain: Feasibility II (week 13) is about a new plant: investment, costs and sales. Sizing cost and beam calculations are parts of a plant's operation, not its overall viability.

questions.q: A ripstop fabric needs its grid of heavy threads spaced correctly. Which lecture covers this?
questions.explain: Design Calculations I — ripstop sizes (week 14) covers exactly this, though its worksheet was not in the course folder, so the page is not reproduced.

questions.q: Because the final is worth 30 marks, a student who skips all quizzes can still obtain an A by scoring full marks in the final.
questions.explain: Skipping quizzes forfeits 25 marks, so the maximum possible total is 75, and in practice missing the quizzes also signals missed lectures and risks the attendance rule.

questions.q: You have the warp in 40 Ne but the weft supplier quotes in tex. Which lecture do you need?
questions.explain: Counting Systems (week 1) links Ne, Nm, tex, dtex and denier through one constant; the other lectures assume the counts are already known.

questions.q: A fabric mixes Ne 30 and Ne 10 ends in a stripe and you need its average count for weight. Which lecture applies?
questions.explain: Multiple Counts II (week 2) weights each count by its number of threads; Multiple Counts I covers only yarns in equal numbers.

questions.q: A student missed week 1 entirely. What is the most sensible first step?
options: Wait for the mid term to see what matters
Study Counting Systems before the next class, since later weeks build on it
Skip to Fabric Production because looms are more interesting
questions.explain: The outline warns that the calculations build on one another week by week; counts are used in nearly every later lecture, so catching up on week 1 first is essential.

questions.q: The sizing department wants its chemical cost per kilogram of warp. Which week covers this?
questions.explain: Sizing Cost Analysis is the first lecture of week 10. Week 3 is fabric weight and sett, week 5 cone size and warping speed, week 14 shed planning and ripstop design.

quizzes.title: Challenge review
quizzes.intro: Harder questions that combine the grading scheme, the lecture plan and the basic units — read each one twice.

questions.q: The plan has 30 slots; one is the mid term and one the overview. How many taught lecture topics remain?
questions.explain: 15 weeks × 2 slots = 30; removing the mid term and the overview leaves 28 taught topics.

questions.q: Of the 30 slots, Shed Planning, Design Calculations I and II and the Overview have no page. How many lecture pages exist besides the mid term?
questions.explain: 30 slots − 1 mid term − 4 without a worksheet = 25 lecture pages (Lectures 01 to 25).

questions.q: Two students: Ali has 10 + 10 + 25 + 10 + 20 and Sara has 5 + 5 + 15 + 25 + 28. Who has the higher total and by how much?
questions.explain: Ali: 10 + 10 + 25 + 10 + 20 = 75; Sara: 5 + 5 + 15 + 25 + 28 = 78. Sara leads by 3 despite weaker participation and assignments.

questions.q: A student has attended 20 of the first 24 lectures. How many of the remaining 6 must she attend to finish at or above 80 %?
questions.explain: She needs 24 of 30 in total; she has 20, so 4 more are required (24 attended ÷ 30 = 80 %). Missing 3 of the last 6 gives 23/30 = 76.7 %.

questions.q: A yarn gives 40 hanks of 840 yd per pound. Which statement is correct?
options: It is Ne 40 and finer than Ne 20
It is Ne 40 and coarser than Ne 20
It is 40 tex and finer than 20 tex
It is Ne 20 because 40 hanks weigh half a pound
questions.explain: Hanks per pound is the Ne definition, so the yarn is Ne 40; in an indirect system a higher number means a finer yarn. Tex works the other way round.

questions.q: The weeks on crimp come after the mid term, so crimp cannot appear in the final exam.
questions.explain: The final comes at the end of the course and covers the whole syllabus; Crimp I and II (weeks 8 and 9) fall after the mid term but well before the final.

questions.q: Which sequence correctly orders these topics as they appear in the plan?
options: Cone Size → Reed Calculations → Beam Calculations → Fabric Production
Beam Calculations → Cone Size → Reed Calculations → Fabric Production
Reed Calculations → Beam Calculations → Cone Size → Fabric Production
Fabric Production → Cone Size → Beam Calculations → Reed Calculations
questions.explain: Beam Calculations is week 4, Cone Size week 5, Reed Calculations week 6 and Fabric Production week 7.

questions.q: A warp uses 1,500 lb of yarn. Express this in maunds, taking 1 lb = 0.4536 kg and 1 maund = 40 kg. Answer to two decimal places.
A classmate says that in tex, like Ne, a bigger number means a finer yarn. What is wrong?
options: Tex is direct: a bigger number means a coarser yarn
Tex is indirect but measured in grams
Ne is direct, so the statement is reversed for Ne
questions.explain: Tex is grams per 1,000 m, a direct system, so the number grows with coarseness. Ne (hanks per pound) is indirect and grows with fineness.

questions.q: Which lecture would you combine with Fabric Production to find how many looms a monthly order needs?
questions.explain: Fabric Production gives metres per loom per day; Planning IV spreads that over months against the order. Counts, crimp and cone size do not give loom numbers.
